A  Beneath the floor of almost any forest lies a dense web of extremely fine fungal threads, called hyphae, which spread through the soil and wrap around or penetrate the roots of plants. Many of these fungi form partnerships with plants known as mycorrhizas, a term derived from the Greek words for 'fungus' and 'root'. The great majority of land plant species are thought to form such partnerships, which are believed to have existed for more than four hundred million years and may have helped the first plants to colonise dry land.

B  The basis of the relationship is an exchange. Plants produce sugars through photosynthesis and pass a portion of them to the fungi, which cannot make their own food. In return, the fungal threads, which are far thinner than roots and can reach into tiny spaces in the soil, gather water and mineral nutrients, especially phosphorus and nitrogen, and transfer them to the plant. Experiments have shown that plants with mycorrhizal partners often grow faster and resist drought and disease better than those without.

C  Because a single fungus can connect to several plants, and a single plant to several fungi, these partnerships can create what scientists call common mycorrhizal networks. In the 1990s, a widely reported study in a Canadian forest used carbon isotopes to show that carbon appeared to move between birch and fir trees, possibly through shared fungi. Popular accounts soon described the network as a 'wood wide web' through which trees share resources, send warning signals and even support their offspring. Some writers described large, old 'mother trees' as nurturing younger trees growing in their shade.

D  These ideas have captured the public imagination, inspiring books, documentaries and even films. In recent years, however, a number of researchers have argued that the popular story has gone well beyond the evidence. A review of the field published in 2023 concluded that although common mycorrhizal networks certainly exist, there is limited evidence from field studies that they are widespread in forests, that significant amounts of resources travel through them, or that this transfer benefits seedlings. Some studies that were often cited as supporting the idea had, according to the reviewers, been interpreted too generously.

E  Part of the difficulty is methodological. Fungal threads are microscopic, the soil is opaque, and it is extremely hard to prove that a substance found in one plant travelled there through a fungus rather than through the soil or the roots themselves. Experiments in which seedlings are separated from neighbouring trees by fine mesh, which blocks roots but allows hyphae to pass, have produced mixed results. Critics also point out that fungi are organisms with their own interests; from an evolutionary perspective, there is no obvious reason why a fungus would transport resources to benefit a tree unless it gained something in return.

F  None of this means that mycorrhizal fungi are unimportant. On the contrary, there is overwhelming evidence that they are essential to the health of most ecosystems, to the cycling of nutrients and to the storage of carbon in the soil. Forest managers increasingly recognise that practices such as heavy machinery use and the removal of all trees from an area can damage fungal communities, slowing the recovery of a forest. The debate is not about whether fungi matter, but about how they function and how cautiously scientists should communicate uncertain findings to the public.

Letting Nature Take Charge

A  Conservation has traditionally involved careful management: protecting particular species, maintaining habitats in a fixed condition and often working hard to prevent natural change. This approach has achieved a great deal, but it is expensive, and it can leave nature permanently dependent on human effort. Rewilding takes a different approach. Its central idea is that, wherever possible, natural processes should be restored and allowed to shape landscapes with minimal human direction. In my view, this shift represents one of the most promising developments in conservation in recent decades, although it is not without its difficulties.

B  Rewilding can take many forms. At one end of the scale, it involves reintroducing large animals that have disappeared from a region, such as wolves, lynx or bison. At the other, it may simply mean ceasing to farm a piece of land and allowing vegetation to develop on its own. Many projects focus on restoring processes rather than particular outcomes: allowing rivers to flood and change course, letting dead trees decay where they fall, and introducing grazing animals whose feeding creates a varied patchwork of open ground, scrub and woodland.

C  One of the most frequently cited examples is the return of grey wolves to Yellowstone National Park in the United States in 1995. According to the popular account, the wolves reduced the number of elk and changed their behaviour, allowing trees along rivers to recover, which in turn benefited beavers, birds and fish. Later studies have shown that the real story is more complicated, with factors such as hunting by humans, other predators and drought also playing a part. I believe the example is still valuable, but it should be presented honestly, as evidence that large predators can influence ecosystems rather than as proof that they always transform them.

D  In densely populated Europe, rewilding has often taken place on a smaller scale. On a former farming estate in southern England, for instance, the owners stopped growing crops and allowed free-roaming cattle, ponies, pigs and deer to graze across the land. Within two decades, the estate had become home to several rare species, including birds that had become scarce elsewhere in the country. Visitors now pay to walk the land and see its wildlife, providing an income that partly replaces the money once earned from crops. Projects of this kind show that rewilding does not require vast wilderness areas, and that private landowners can make an important contribution. They also suggest that the results of rewilding can appear far more quickly than many ecologists had expected.

E  Critics raise several objections, and some deserve serious attention. Farmers worry about the loss of productive land and about predators attacking livestock. Rural communities may feel that decisions are being imposed by outsiders who do not depend on the land for their living. These concerns are legitimate, and in my opinion projects that ignore them are likely to fail. Successful rewilding requires early consultation with local people, fair compensation for losses and, ideally, new sources of income, for example from nature tourism.

F  Other critics argue that rewilding is unscientific because its outcomes are unpredictable. I find this argument unconvincing. Uncertainty is not a reason to avoid action, particularly when the alternative is continued loss of biodiversity. The Silk Roads: Networks of Exchange

A  The term 'Silk Road' conjures up images of camel caravans crossing deserts loaded with precious fabrics. Yet the name itself is relatively modern: it was coined in 1877 by a German geographer, more than four centuries after the great age of overland trade between China and the Mediterranean had ended. Historians today often prefer to speak of 'Silk Roads' in the plural, because the routes formed a shifting network of paths across mountains, deserts and grasslands rather than a single highway, and because silk was only one of many goods carried along them.

B  Trade across Central Asia existed long before any empire organised it, but the Chinese Han dynasty played a major role in expanding it. In the second century BCE, the imperial envoy Zhang Qian travelled westward on diplomatic missions in search of allies against nomadic peoples to the north. His reports of wealthy kingdoms and fine horses in Central Asia encouraged the Han court to extend its control along the corridor of oases that leads westward from China. Chinese silk soon reached the Roman world, where it became so fashionable that some Roman writers complained about the amount of money leaving the empire to pay for it.

C  Very few individuals ever travelled the entire length of these routes. Instead, goods typically passed through many hands, moving from one trading city to the next. Merchants from Sogdiana, a region centred on what is now Uzbekistan, became particularly important intermediaries, establishing communities in towns from Central Asia to northern China. Along the way, travellers stayed at caravanserais, fortified inns where people, animals and goods could rest safely overnight. Many of these buildings still stand today.

D  The goods exchanged were remarkably varied. China exported silk, ceramics and later paper, while Central Asia supplied horses, and India contributed cotton textiles, spices and precious stones. Glassware from the Mediterranean world has been found in Chinese tombs, and silver vessels from Persia have been discovered as far east as Japan. Plants also travelled: grapes, alfalfa and walnuts are among the crops thought to have reached China from the west, while peaches and apricots spread in the opposite direction.

E  Perhaps more important than any physical goods were the ideas, beliefs and technologies that spread along the routes. Buddhism travelled from India through Central Asia into China, where it eventually became one of the major religions. Missionaries, pilgrims and translators followed the trade routes, and cave temples decorated with Buddhist paintings and sculptures were created at oasis towns along the way. Technologies such as papermaking moved westward, while musical instruments, artistic styles and astronomical knowledge were exchanged in both directions.

F  Not everything that travelled along the routes was beneficial. Many historians believe that the plague which devastated Europe and the Middle East in the fourteenth century, known as the Black Death, spread at least partly along trade routes connecting Central Asia with the Black Sea. The same connections that brought wealth and new ideas could also transmit disease with terrible speed.

G  From the fifteenth century onwards, overland trade declined in importance. Political fragmentation made the routes less secure, and European sailors established direct sea routes to Asia, which could carry larger quantities of goods more cheaply. Today, however, the Silk Roads have regained symbolic importance. Parts of the network have been recognised as World Heritage sites, and modern infrastructure projects frequently borrow the name, presenting new railways and ports as the heirs of an ancient tradition of exchange.

A  The term 'Silk Road' conjures up images of camel caravans crossing deserts loaded with precious fabrics. Yet the name itself is relatively modern: it was coined in 1877 by a German geographer, more than four centuries after the great age of overland trade between China and the Mediterranean had ended. Historians today often prefer to speak of 'Silk Roads' in the plural, because the routes formed a shifting network of paths across mountains, deserts and grasslands rather than a single highway, and because silk was only one of many goods carried along them.

B  Trade across Central Asia existed long before any empire organised it, but the Chinese Han dynasty played a major role in expanding it. In the second century BCE, the imperial envoy Zhang Qian travelled westward on diplomatic missions in search of allies against nomadic peoples to the north. His reports of wealthy kingdoms and fine horses in Central Asia encouraged the Han court to extend its control along the corridor of oases that leads westward from China. Chinese silk soon reached the Roman world, where it became so fashionable that some Roman writers complained about the amount of money leaving the empire to pay for it.

C  Very few individuals ever travelled the entire length of these routes. Instead, goods typically passed through many hands, moving from one trading city to the next. Merchants from Sogdiana, a region centred on what is now Uzbekistan, became particularly important intermediaries, establishing communities in towns from Central Asia to northern China. Along the way, travellers stayed at caravanserais, fortified inns where people, animals and goods could rest safely overnight. Many of these buildings still stand today.

D  The goods exchanged were remarkably varied. China exported silk, ceramics and later paper, while Central Asia supplied horses, and India contributed cotton textiles, spices and precious stones. Glassware from the Mediterranean world has been found in Chinese tombs, and silver vessels from Persia have been discovered as far east as Japan. Plants also travelled: grapes, alfalfa and walnuts are among the crops thought to have reached China from the west, while peaches and apricots spread in the opposite direction.

E  Perhaps more important than any physical goods were the ideas, beliefs and technologies that spread along the routes. Buddhism travelled from India through Central Asia into China, where it eventually became one of the major religions. Missionaries, pilgrims and translators followed the trade routes, and cave temples decorated with Buddhist paintings and sculptures were created at oasis towns along the way. Technologies such as papermaking moved westward, while musical instruments, artistic styles and astronomical knowledge were exchanged in both directions.

F  Not everything that travelled along the routes was beneficial. Many historians believe that the plague which devastated Europe and the Middle East in the fourteenth century, known as the Black Death, spread at least partly along trade routes connecting Central Asia with the Black Sea. The same connections that brought wealth and new ideas could also transmit disease with terrible speed.

G  From the fifteenth century onwards, overland trade declined in importance. Political fragmentation made the routes less secure, and European sailors established direct sea routes to Asia, which could carry larger quantities of goods more cheaply. Today, however, the Silk Roads have regained symbolic importance. Parts of the network have been recognised as World Heritage sites, and modern infrastructure projects frequently borrow the name, presenting new railways and ports as the heirs of an ancient tradition of exchange.
